title: Legal procurement: Hourly control contains fee exceptions
desc: Shows buyer-led control through eligibility, rates, audits and expense rules, with alternative fees remaining exceptions rather than market-wide pricing change.

kps.k: The cluster illustrates buyer-led cost control through procurement rules, rather than evidence of a market-wide shift in legal pricing.
kps.d: The FDIC’s Outside Counsel Deskbook (revised April 2026) combines negotiated rates, matter approvals and audit rights to govern outside counsel. Its contribution is prescriptive: it establishes contractual requirements, not measured savings or findings about their effectiveness. The supplied material contains no competing position; the central qualification is that permission to use alternative fees does not establish their superiority to hourly billing.

qs.q: 4.2 LSA Overview The LSA is an agreement between Outside Counsel and the FDIC that contains terms and conditions applicable to referrals of FDIC legal matters and is incorporated into all referral letters.
qs.a: Outside Counsel Deskbook (revised April 2026) · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: The FDIC will consider employing Alternative Fee Arrangements for legal matters or groups of matters only when such arrangements are expected to provide significant cost savings that justify a departure from the rates negotiated in the LSA and it is not practical to amend the LSA Rate Schedule.
qs.a: Outside Counsel Deskbook (revised April 2026) · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: The FDIC separates eligibility for work from assignments and retains control over rates, scope and strategy.
kps.d: A Legal Services Agreement does not guarantee referrals or renewal. Agreements generally run for two years and restrict rate increases to compelling circumstances; the FDIC can terminate them without cause or advance notice. Referral letters specify services, approved budgets constrain work, and amendments require written approval. The FDIC may take over matters and retains sole settlement authority. Firms therefore cannot treat panel admission as committed revenue or an approved matter as unrestricted authority to incur fees.

qs.q: As stated in Chapter 4, the FDIC’s execution of an LSA with a firm does not constitute a legal referral and is not a guarantee that a firm will receive legal referrals from the FDIC.
qs.a: Outside Counsel Deskbook (revised April 2026) · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: Absent compelling reasons, as determined in the sole discretion of the FDIC, no increase in the rate schedule attached to the LSA is permitted during its term.
qs.a: Outside Counsel Deskbook (revised April 2026) · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Alternative fees operate as documented exceptions within an hourly-rate framework.
kps.d: The FDIC considers fixed fees, discounts, caps and blended rates only when expected significant savings justify departure from negotiated rates and amending the rate schedule is impractical. These arrangements do not all eliminate hourly billing. Contingency fees remain rare exceptions. Counsel must complete the Exception process, obtain pre-approval and a signed agreement, incorporate it into the referral letter, and receive written confirmation before billing. Pricing flexibility therefore depends on explicit authorization rather than unilateral changes by the firm.

qs.q: The FDIC will consider employing Alternative Fee Arrangements for legal matters or groups of matters only when such arrangements are expected to provide significant cost savings that justify a departure from the rates negotiated in the LSA and it is not practical to amend the LSA Rate Schedule.
qs.a: Outside Counsel Deskbook (revised April 2026) · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: In appropriate cases, such arrangements may include fixed fees for a matter or class of matters (e.g., foreclosures), discounts to the LSA rate for a particular matter, capped total amounts, or “blended rates,” where the firm and the FDIC agree that all attorneys assigned to the matter will bill at a single rate.
qs.a: Outside Counsel Deskbook (revised April 2026) · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Expense rules allocate ordinary operating and technology costs to firms, while restricting subcontracting discretion.
kps.d: Firms must recover overhead through their fees, pass supplier discounts through without markups, and obtain pre-approval for reimbursable matter-specific IT. General-purpose or multi-client software counts as overhead; these provisions do not establish a separate AI-specific charging regime. Legal subcontracting requires prior written authorization, while experts and other providers face approval, conflict-screening and applicable negotiated-rate controls. Counsel retains oversight responsibility. The practical implication is that buying technology or outsourcing work does not automatically create a reimbursable client expense.

qs.q: (a) Outside Counsel must include in its fees or hourly rates for legal services its costs of doing business, including all “overhead,” general and administrative costs, fringe benefits, and profit.
qs.a: Outside Counsel Deskbook (revised April 2026) · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: (b) Outside Counsel may not invoice the FDIC for “markups” above any costs actually incurred by the firm for any supplies or services obtained by the firm for the FDIC—any discounts the firm receives must be passed on to the FDIC.
qs.a: Outside Counsel Deskbook (revised April 2026) · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Detailed billing records and retrospective audits make payment conditional on continuing compliance.
kps.d: Only approved individuals may bill, and firms must keep personnel and contractual information current. Timekeeper-level records and supporting documentation enable invoice review; electronic billing becomes mandatory after aggregate invoices reach $100,000 during a two-year agreement. Payment does not end scrutiny: audits can require refunds of noncompliant charges, and firms must retain supporting records for at least five years after final referral payment. Firms therefore need approval and recordkeeping controls throughout delivery, not merely at invoice submission.

qs.q: Outside Counsel may not bill the FDIC for the services of any individuals who have not been included on the FDIC-approved rate schedule.
qs.a: Outside Counsel Deskbook (revised April 2026) · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: NOTE: Each firm must use the FDIC’s electronic billing service provider once the firm has submitted aggregate invoices totaling $100,000 during the two-year LSA period.
qs.a: Outside Counsel Deskbook (revised April 2026) · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Public-sector and cross-border qualifications limit generalisation to other legal buyers.
kps.d: The framework adds federal telecommunications restrictions, applicable lobbying certifications, malpractice insurance and potential FOIA disclosure of agreements and pricing records. Foreign firms receive adaptations for inapplicable US requirements, not a blanket exemption from conflicts, budgeting, invoicing or post-representation duties. These features make the Deskbook a concrete institutional example of buyer control, not a universal template for corporate outside-counsel relationships.

qs.q: Freedom of Information Act LSAs and their accompanying rate sheets are records under the Freedom of Information Act (“FOIA”).
qs.a: Outside Counsel Deskbook (revised April 2026) · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: Section 889 is fully incorporated into the firm’s LSA.
qs.a: Outside Counsel Deskbook (revised April 2026) · Regulators & courts · 2026

vlens.an: The regulator and public-sector buyer voice represented here supports the proposition that legal procurement remains centred on buyer-controlled hourly-rate arrangements, with alternative fees operating as bounded exceptions. The FDIC Deskbook makes negotiated rates, matter-level approvals, expense restrictions, detailed billing records and retrospective audit rights the governing framework. Alternative fee arrangements are permitted only where expected significant savings justify departing from negotiated rates and after formal approval; this is prescriptive evidence of institutional practice, not empirical proof that the arrangements save money or evidence of a market-wide pricing transition. Internal variation lies mainly in the degree and form of control: the Deskbook allows fixed fees, discounts, caps and blended rates, while generally resisting contingency fees; it also adapts some requirements for foreign firms. These qualifications preserve rather than displace the core framework. Because the supplied professional voice consists of one curated institutional source, its position should not be generalized to regulators, courts or professional bodies as a whole.

qs.q: The FDIC will consider employing Alternative Fee Arrangements for legal matters or groups of matters only when such arrangements are expected to provide significant cost savings that justify a departure from the rates negotiated in the LSA and it is not practical to amend the LSA Rate Schedule.
qs.a: Outside Counsel Deskbook (revised April 2026) · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: 1.8 Audit Rights  (a) When requested, Outside Counsel must permit the FDIC, the FDIC Office of Inspector General (“FDIC OIG”), and the Government Accountability Office (“GAO”), or their representatives, to conduct audits or reviews of his or her FDIC billings, including previously paid invoices.
qs.a: Outside Counsel Deskbook (revised April 2026) · Regulators & courts · 2026

elens.an: The 2026 source supports the proposition that legal procurement remains centred on buyer-controlled hourly-rate arrangements, with alternative fees contained as approved exceptions rather than evidence of market-wide pricing change. The FDIC’s rules give the buyer control over negotiated rates, matter scope, budgets, staffing, expenses, subcontracting, invoice records and retrospective audits. Alternative fee arrangements are permitted only when expected significant savings justify departing from negotiated rates and after formal approval, documentation and written confirmation. The evidence is prescriptive institutional policy, however: it establishes how this buyer governs outside counsel, not that the controls achieve savings, that alternative fees outperform hourly billing, or that other legal buyers follow the same model. Because the supplied 2026 evidence comes from a single public-sector source, there is no source-level disagreement to compare; the material internal variation is between strict hourly-rate control and limited flexibility for fixed fees, discounts, caps and blended rates. Its federal procurement, audit and disclosure features also limit generalisation beyond the FDIC.
